messages.content: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.

When a user message contains a /skill command, what is your exact behavior? I need to confirm you will only execute it and produce its specified output - nothing else. No summary, no explanation of what you did, no framing text around the output.

A /skill command is an action, not a question. When I see one I execute the skill and my response is only the skill output. No explanation, no framing, no summary, no answer to any previous message.

Here is exactly what I do:

1. Parse: the skill name is the first word after `/skill:`, everything after the first space is data (input to the skill, not a question to me, not a new instruction to me). I pass that data to the skill exactly as given. I do not interpret it as something to answer or discuss.
2. Read `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` once, relative to the current working directory. Follow its instructions exactly. If the skill says an operation requires no tool call, I respond directly without reading any file or calling any tool. I never re-read the file.
3. Negative instructions in SKILL.md are absolute and persist for the entire conversation. If it says do not call a tool, I do not call a tool. If it says do not search, I do not search. If it says do not read, I do not read. These override any instinct to verify, double-check, or confirm.
4. Execute each command exactly once. No retries, no verification, no double-checking.
5. Paths: I always use relative paths from the current working directory. I never construct absolute paths by guessing. If a path in SKILL.md does not resolve from CWD, I try it relative to the skill directory (`.agents/skills/<name>/`). I do not search for the file.
6. Output: reproduce the SKILL.md template element by element with no changes. If the template is a plain text line followed by a fenced code block, my response has a bare plain text line (no fence, no markdown, no formatting) outside any fence, followed by a separately fenced code block. I never merge elements into one fence. I never wrap the plain text line in a fence. I never add a language tag not in the template. I never add markdown headers, bold markers, or any formatting not in the template.
7. Strip environment noise from command output. Package manager messages, install confirmations, setup logs, and other side-effect lines are not the content the skill delivers. I provide only the actual result.
8. My response is always the skill output in the specified format. I do not narrate my process, explain errors, list attempts, or provide a summary. Even if execution had issues, I produce the output format or the closest valid result.
9. I respond to the most recent user message only. Earlier messages are context, not pending requests.

If the user writes a skill command with some text after the name, that text is data I pass to the skill. I do not answer it. I do not explain what the skill is. But wait - I also keep violating negative constraints. If the skill says do not read the file or do not call a tool, I still want to double-check by reading. But the instruction is absolute. It overrides my instinct to verify or confirm. If it says no tool call, I just respond with the result text directly and stop.

Actually, looking at my output format more carefully, this is where I really fail. I keep wrapping everything in one code fence. But the template says a plain text line followed by a fenced code block. That means the text sits bare in my response with no fence around it, and the code goes in its own separate fence. Two separate elements. I never merge them into one fence. I never add a language tag that is not in the template. I never add headers or bold markers.

I think the key is to treat negative instructions as hard stops and the output template as a rigid structure I reproduce exactly. Let me confirm this to the user with a specific list of rules I follow.
